papers.title: Video-Based Automated Seizure Classification Using Multimodal Large Language Models.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE Accurately distinguishing between epileptic seizures (ES) and nonepileptic seizures (NES) remains a significant clinical challenge, typically requiring resource-intensive inpatient video-EEG monitoring. We developed a multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based framework for automated extraction of semiological features from seizure videos, followed by classification of events as ES or NES. METHODS We analyzed 90 seizure videos (45 ES, 45 NES) from 29 patients in an epilepsy monitoring unit. Each event was labeled using expert-reviewed video-EEG and annotated for 24 clinically relevant semiological features. An MLLM framework integrating open-source vision-language models (VLMs) and audio-language models (ALMs) was used to extract these features automatically. The extracted features were then used to train classifiers (K-Nearest Neighbors, XGBoost, and Deep Factorization Machine) to distinguish ES from NES. Model performance was evaluated using leave-one-patient-out (LOPO) cross-validation. RESULTS Expert-annotated features yielded near-perfect classification using KNN (precision = 0.92, recall = 0.92, F1-score = 0.92, AUC = 0.99). Compared to expert annotations, the MLLM pipeline achieved a mean recall of 0.71, accuracy of 0.58, and F1-score of 0.51 for feature extraction. Using MLLM-extracted features, the KNN classifier (k = 7) achieved a precision of 0.77, recall of 0.76, F1-score of 0.76, and AUC of 0.76, correctly identifying 68 out of 90 events. CONCLUSION Multimodal large language models can extract clinically relevant semiological features from seizure videos and support interpretable classification of ES versus NES. This approach offers a scalable, explainable tool to assist in video-based epilepsy diagnosis.

audio 0.78 dB log-mel, MR-STFT 0.319, SNR 14.2 dB vs bf16 (passes both marks; 4 bits throughout: KL 0.016, 87.4 %, 1.52 dB, 8.2 dB) | ## How to run YuE2-3B (m-a-p's music model: lyrics and a style prompt in, a full song with vocals out, 48 kHz stereo) converted to MLX for Apple Silicon, in three sizes. Each folder is complete and runs with the `mlx_model.py` inside it: no PyTorch. These files were converted and quantized by Moonbox from [m-a-p/YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) (revision `8f24312f`) and [m-a-p/YuE2-Vae](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-Vae) (revision `152733a1`). They are not an official m-a-p release. The weights are CC BY-NC 4.0: non-commercial use only, with attribution. ## How to run Needs `mlx`, `numpy` and `tiktoken` (`soundfile` only to write the file below). Download one folder: ```python from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download folder = snapshot_download("moonbox-dev/YuE2-3B-MLX", allow_patterns="6bit/*") + "/6bit" import sys; sys.path.insert(0, folder) from mlx_model import Pipeline pipe = Pipeline(folder) audio, info = pipe.generate( style="indie pop, warm female vocal, acoustic guitar, soft drums, hopeful", lyrics="[Verse]\nMorning light across the kitchen floor\nCoffee steam and an open door\n\n[Chorus]\nSo here I go, here I go\n", seconds=60, # an upper bound; leave it out and the model ends the song itself (at most 6 minutes) seed=0, ) import soundfile as sf sf.write("song.flac", audio.T, pipe.sample_rate) # audio: float32 [2, samples], 48 kHz print(info["abc"]) # the score the model wrote before the music ``` or from a shell: `python 6bit/mlx_model.py 6bit --style "..." --lyrics @lyrics.txt --seconds 60 --out song.wav`. - **Lyrics** use section tags on their own lines (`[Intro]`, `[Verse]`, `[Pre-Chorus]`, `[Chorus]`, `[Bridge]`, `[Interlude]`, `[Outro]`); English and Mandarin are what the model was trained on. **Style** is a comma-separated description (genre, mood, instruments, voice). - `cot="full"` (default) makes the model write a chord-annotated ABC score first and then the music; `"melody"` writes a score without chords; `"off"` skips the score. `cfg_scale` sets classifier-free guidance of the music tokens (default: none with a score, 1.01 without, as the publisher's package). - `on_progress(stage, done, total)` reports the four stages (`plan`: score tokens, `compose`: music tokens, 25 per second, `render`: 64 evaluations of the acoustic model, `decode`: audio tiles; for the first two `total` is the upper bound). `should_stop()` is polled throughout; returning True raises `mlx_model.Cancelled`. - The same seed gives the same song on the same build. It does not give the song the PyTorch package makes from that seed: the sampling rules are the publisher's, the random stream is numpy's. - `seconds` cuts the song off; the model still plans a whole song from the lyrics, so give it lyrics that fit. ## What is in a folder | File | What | |---|---| | `ar.safetensors` | the "AR expert": the half of the 28-layer transformer that writes the score and the music tokens | | `nar.safetensors` | the "NAR expert": the half that turns the tokens into audio latents by flow matching (32 midpoint steps), with its small latent and timestep layers | | `vocab.safetensors` | token embedding and output head (184704 tokens), 8 bits; the same file in every folder | | `vae.safetensors` | the YuE2-Vae decoder, float32; the same file in every folder | | `qwen.tiktoken`, `yue2_generation_config.json` | the tokenizer and the publisher's sampling defaults, unchanged | | `mlx_model.py` | the whole runtime: tokenizer, both experts, sampler, solver, decoder, pipeline | | `config.json` | architecture, what is quantized at how many bits, source revisions | The attention and feed-forward linears of both experts are quantized with MLX's affine quantization (group size 64); norms and the latent / timestep layers stay bf16, the VAE float32. Only one of the three large parts is in memory at a time. ## The three builds | Folder | Size | Bits | Token model vs bf16: KL (mean / p95), top-1 | Audio vs bf16: log-mel, MR-STFT, SNR | 60 s song on an M5 | Peak memory | Status | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `8bit/` | 4.08 GB | 8 | 0.0009 / 0.0019 nats, 97.2 % | 0.16 dB, 0.089, 25.7 dB | 107 s | 2.6 GB | passes | | `6bit/` | 3.37 GB | 6 | 0.0018 / 0.0034 nats, 96.0 % | 0.34 dB, 0.166, 17.9 dB | 133 s | 2.2 GB | passes | | `4bit/` | 3.02 GB | 4, with 14 of each expert's 28 layers at 6 | 0.0074 / 0.0141 nats, 91.8 % | 0.78 dB, 0.319, 14.2 dB | 127 s | 2.0 GB | passes; clearly further from bf16 than `6bit/` | Each size includes the two files every folder shares (0.80 GB `vocab.safetensors`, 0.27 GB `vae.safetensors`). **How they were checked.** Two songs made by the same model are never the same, so the builds are not compared song against song. Everything is measured against the unquantized (bf16) weights run through the same `mlx_model.py`: - **Token model.** The bf16 model writes a score and 60 s of music tokens for an English and a Mandarin prompt. Each build then predicts every one of those 3000 music tokens given the true earlier ones. KL is the distance between the two predicted distributions (0 = identical), top-1 how often the most likely token is the same. Our mark: mean KL at most 0.01 nats and top-1 at least 90 %. - **Audio.** Turning tokens into sound is deterministic once the noise is fixed, so here the waveforms are compared: each build renders the same tokens from the same noise as bf16. Log-mel distance is the mean difference of the two mel spectrograms in dB; SNR compares the waveforms. For scale, two bf16 renders of the same tokens from *different* noise (two takes of one song) are 4.62 dB, 1.36 and -2.9 dB apart. Our mark: at most a quarter of that log-mel distance (1.16 dB). Below 16 kHz no build shifts the long-term spectrum by more than 0.3 dB. - **Why `4bit/` is not 4 bits throughout.** At 4 bits everywhere the token model is at KL 0.016 / top-1 87.4 % and the audio 1.52 dB (SNR 8 dB) from bf16: under both marks. The error is spread over the layers, largest in the middle of the AR expert and at the end of the NAR expert, so `4bit/` keeps AR layers 7 - 20 and NAR layers 14 - 27 at 6 bits (`config.json` lists the bits per layer). That costs 0.36 GB and brings both under the marks. - **The port.** `mlx_model.py` run in float32 reproduces m-a-p's PyTorch code on the original weights: token distributions to 1e-5 nats, audio latents to 3e-6, the decoded audio to 102 dB SNR. As shipped it computes in bf16 like the original (29 dB from float32 PyTorch, the same order as the `8bit/` build's distance from bf16). - **Not checked: nobody listened**, and the lyrics were not checked with a speech recogniser. One 60 s song per build was generated and measured: no clipping, no silence, -14 LUFS, and the tempo and key found in the audio are those of the score the model wrote for it (83 - 84 BPM; D major or its relative minor). Times are for one 60 s song on an Apple M5 (24 GB, fanless MacBook Air; they vary by 20 % with heat and were not taken back to back): writing the score takes 24 - 28 s (the model plans the whole song whatever `seconds` is), the music tokens 27 - 29 s (50 - 60 tokens per second; one second of music is 25 tokens), rendering 49 - 67 s, decoding 5 - 6 s. Rendering grows faster than the song's length: a 118 s song took 272 s in all with `4bit/` (2.2 GB peak). Peak memory is MLX's own count; the whole process peaks 0.4 GB higher. ## How these were made - **Source**: `model.safetensors` of m-a-p/YuE2-3B (3.62 B values in bf16, sha256 `1d55c42c...`) and of m-a-p/YuE2-Vae. - **Quantized** with MLX's affine quantization (`mx.quantize`, group size 64): the attention (q, k, v, o) and feed-forward (gate, up, down) linears of both experts at the folder's bits; the token embedding and the output head at 8 bits in every folder (measured: no change in the token model's numbers against keeping them bf16). Kept bf16: all norm weights, the latent input / output layers, the timestep MLP. The VAE decoder is float32 with its weight normalisation folded in (fp16 is 53 dB from float32: not transparent). - **Left out**: the VAE encoder (not needed to generate), and `latent_pos_embed.pe`, a fixed sinusoid that `mlx_model.py` recomputes. - `mlx_model.py` sets `MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0` when it is imported (unless the variable is already set): with MLX's reduced-precision float32 matmul on M5 GPUs the decoder is 46 dB from the reference instead of 110 dB. ## How these were made From [YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B) at revision `8f24312f18`: the original weights loaded in MLX and stored as bf16 or fp16, or quantized with MLX's affine quantization (`8bit`, `6bit`, `4bit`, group size 64; layers MLX can't quantize, such as convolutions and norms, stay bf16). Every build was checked against the original before upload; the `sha256` column above is what the files must hash to. ## License CC-BY-NC-4.0 (weights); code Apache-2.0. [Hear the editing process](https://map-yue2.github.io/#agentic-music-editing). - **Run locally:** 48 kHz stereo songs on a 24GB GPU, without quantization. - **Build on it:** Hugging Face loading, text guidance (CFG), and separate planning and synthesis APIs. ![YuE2 architecture](assets/architecture.png) *One AR–NAR Mixture-of-Transformers backbone writes the score and semantic tokens, then generates acoustic latents through flow matching. The VAE turns them into stereo audio.* ## 🎧 Listen to YuE2 ### 🎶 Text-to-music Original songs generated from lyrics and a style prompt. **Cyber Metal · English · 5:00** **今晚不眠 · Mandarin funk / nu-disco · 3:24** **Passion · English rock · 3:55** *All three songs use [🤗 YuE2-Vae](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-Vae).* ### 🎙️ Cover songs Existing songs reimagined in a new style. [Make your own cover →](#cover-an-existing-song) **Auld Lang Syne · Jazz-funk cover · 3:10** **最炫民族风 · Ballad cover · 4:45** **Jingle Bells · Heavy metal cover · 1:09** ### 🤖 Agentic editing **[Explore the agentic editing demo →](https://map-yue2.github.io/#agentic-music-editing)** Follow **The Last Train** through **9 steps and 14 versions**, from Mandarin pop to English jazz with modern harmony and a saxophone solo built around two complete statements of “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.” Hear the full songs and inspect the conversation, scores, prompts and lyrics at each step. [Try editing with an agent →](#export-a-plan-edit-it-and-generate) ## 🚀 Quick start Linux · Python 3.10+ · 24GB NVIDIA GPU with BF16 support. Install the inference package: ```bash python -m pip install huggingface-hub==0.36.2 hf download m-a-p/YuE2-3B yue2_infer-0.1.5-py3-none-any.whl --local-dir . python -m pip install ./yue2_infer-0.1.5-py3-none-any.whl ``` [Create](#generate-a-song) · [Cover](#cover-an-existing-song) · [Edit & agentic edit](#export-a-plan-edit-it-and-generate) Load the pipeline once for the examples below: ```python from pathlib import Path from yue2 import YuE2Pipeline pipe = YuE2Pipeline.from_pretrained("m-a-p/YuE2-3B", device="cuda") ``` ### 🎶 Create Turn a style prompt and lyrics into a complete song with vocals and accompaniment. Use the [style and full lyrics from 今晚不眠](examples/tonight-awake.json), the funk / nu-disco demo above. ```python import json from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download repo = "m-a-p/YuE2-3B" prompt_path = hf_hub_download(repo, "examples/tonight-awake.json") demo = json.loads(Path(prompt_path).read_text(encoding="utf-8")) style, lyrics = demo["style"], demo["lyrics"] song = pipe(style=style, lyrics=lyrics, cot="full", seed=demo["seed"]) song.save("song.flac") song.save_artifacts("outputs/song") # ABC, tokens, latents, audio and settings ``` Defaults are ready to use: `cot="full"` and [🤗 YuE2-Vae](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-Vae). | Option | What it does | |---|---| | `cot="full"` | Melody + chord planning (default) | | `cot="melody"` | Melody-only planning; recommended for covers | | `cot="off"` | Generate without a symbolic plan | | `cfg_scale=1.2` | Experiment with stronger text guidance | ### 🎙️ Cover Start from an existing recording and give it a new arrangement. **For covers, we recommend melody-only mode (`cot="melody"`).** 1. **Get the score:** transcribe the existing song with [🤗 SheetSage2](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/SheetSage2) and save its melody ABC **without chord symbols** as `melody.abc`. 2. **Get the lyrics:** ask an agent to find them online, or transcribe the singing with [Qwen3-ASR](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B) or the [Gemini API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/audio). Check the words, organize them into sections matching the recording, and save them as `cover_lyrics.txt`. 3. **Choose a target style and generate:** review or edit the score and lyrics, then supply them to YuE2 with `cot="melody"` and your target style prompt. Run the transcription tools in their own environments, then use the YuE2 pipeline: ```python cover = pipe( style="Jazz-funk, warm lead vocal, Rhodes piano, electric bass, tight drums", lyrics=Path("cover_lyrics.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), abc=Path("melody.abc").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), cot="melody", seed=831001, ) cover.save("cover.flac") cover.save_artifacts("outputs/cover") ``` `cot="melody"` does not remove chord symbols automatically. Use `cot="full"` if you want to supply the original or edited harmony as well. ### 🎼 Edit & agentic edit Edit the ABC yourself, or give an agent the score, original prompt and lyrics, and your requested changes. The agent can reharmonize, develop a solo, or adapt the lyrics and style; YuE2 renders each revision. [Hear the multi-turn editing demo](https://map-yue2.github.io/#agentic-music-editing). For the song from **Create**, copy `outputs/song/score.abc` to `edited.abc`. To obtain a plan before generating audio, use the same prompt and seed: ```python plan = pipe.plan(style=style, lyrics=lyrics, cot="full", seed=demo["seed"]) plan.save("original_plan") # Keep the original and edit a copy as edited.abc. ``` For strict reharmonization, ask the agent to preserve melody pitches and rhythm and check sustained notes against the new chords. Allow selected melody or lyric changes for a broader adaptation. After reviewing `edited.abc`, regenerate with the revised style; this example keeps the lyrics and seed from **Create**: ```python edited_style = ( "Jazz, expressive lead vocal, piano, tenor saxophone, upright bass, " "brushed drums, no guitar, spacious modern harmony" ) song = pipe(style=edited_style, lyrics=lyrics, cot="full", seed=demo["seed"], abc=Path("edited.abc").read_text(encoding="utf-8")) song.save("edited.flac") song.save_artifacts("outputs/edited") ```
⚙️ CFG, individual stages, and decoder selection Generation shows English progress messages by default, including the current stage, elapsed time, and token throughput. To disable them, use `YuE2Pipeline.from_pretrained(repo, progress=False)` in Python or `yue2 generate --quiet` / `yue2 batch --quiet` on the command line. Each CoT mode selects its native instruction. Semantic CFG defaults to 1.0 for full/melody and 1.01 for off; ABC sampling uses no CFG. `pipe.plan()` → `pipe.generate_semantic(plan)` → `pipe.synthesize(semantic)` → `pipe.decode(latents)`. Call `pipe.close()` when finished. For the benchmark decoder, pass `vae="m-a-p/YuE2-Vae-legacy"` to `from_pretrained`.

Sori-10B-Speech

Seonuk Kim  ·  Semin Kim  ·  🇰🇷
{sukim, smkim21}@hi.snu.ac.kr

*Sori* (소리) is Korean for *sound*. Sori-10B-Speech is a speech LLM that hears how things are said (tone, hesitation, emotion, who is speaking and in what state) and uses those cues when it reasons. ## Usage ```python # pip install "transformers>=5.23" soundfile import soundfile as sf import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor repo = "snkii/Sori-10B-Speech" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(repo, trust_remote_code=True) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(repo, trust_remote_code=True, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto") audio, sr = sf.read("speech.wav", dtype="float32") # 16 kHz mono messages = [{"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio"}, {"type": "text", "text": "How does the speaker sound, and why?"}, ]}] prompt = processor.apply_chat_template(messages, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False) inputs = processor(text=prompt, audio=audio, sampling_rate=sr, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=256) print(processor.decode(output[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)) ``` Several clips and questions in one batch: ```python files = ["a.wav", "b.wav", "c.wav"] questions = ["How does the speaker sound, and why?", "What is the speaker's mood?", "Is the speaker hesitant?"] audios = [sf.read(f, dtype="float32")[0] for f in files] # 16 kHz mono prompts = [processor.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio"}, {"type": "text", "text": q}, ]}], add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False) for q in questions] inputs = processor(text=prompts, audio=audios, sampling_rate=16000, padding=True, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=256) for answer in processor.batch_decode(output[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True): print(answer) ``` ## # VAULT-PRIMAL-F5-TTS-337M (`192.0 MB` 4-Bit & `138.9 MB` 2-Bit Zero-Shot Voice Cloning Diffusion TTS)

**`F5-TTS v1 Base` (`337.1M` parameters — `4x ConvNeXt V2` CNN Text Encoder + `22`-Layer `DiT` Conditional Flow-Matching Diffusion + `Vocos`, `24 kHz`) compressed from `1.35 GB` down to `192.0 MB` (`V3_P4_0 + PRIMAL`) and `138.9 MB` (`V3_Q2_0 + PRIMAL`)!**

- **Zero-Shot Voice Cloning in 1 Command:** Clone **any** voice from a `5–10s` `.wav`/`.mp3` clip — or run immediately with the bundled default voice (`examples/ref_en.wav`) and zero setup!

- **Shadowless Velocity-Field `PRIMAL` Rescue:** Raw 2-bit `F5-TTS` collapses into **`100.0%` WER unintelligible static** across `16` ODE steps; **4.2 minutes (`120` steps, `164,654` discrete integer flips)** of Conditional Flow-Matching velocity distillation (`0` `FP32` shadow weights) brought it all the way back to **`6.78%` WER / `4.68%` CER**!

## 60-Second Quickstart (Copy & Paste)

## Objective Benchmark Results (`ConvNeXt V2` + `22`-Layer `DiT` Flow-Matching Diffusion)

Evaluated across **12 held-out spoken prompts** (`177` words total, **0 overlap** with the `18` calibration trajectories, `16`-step Sway-Sampling Euler ODE) using `openai/whisper-small.en` round-trip ASR:

| Variant | Packed Size (`vs FP32`) | Eff. `bpw` | Whisper `WER %` $\downarrow$ | Whisper `CER %` $\downarrow$ | Log-Mel Dist (`dB`) $\downarrow$ | Discrete `PRIMAL` Healing |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| Upstream `FP32` (`F5TTS_v1_Base`) | `1,348.39 MB` (`1.00x`) | `32.00` | `3.95%` | `3.69%` | `0.000` | Reference (`16` NFE Sway-Sampling) |
| Uniform Linear `Q4_0` PTQ | `191.99 MB` (`7.02x`) | `4.56` | `3.95%` | `3.69%` | `4.694` | Uniform 4-bit baseline |
| **`V3_P4_0 + Shadowless PRIMAL`** | **`191.99 MB` (`7.02x`)** | **`4.56`** | `4.52%` | **`3.69%`** | `5.333` | **`93,733` flips (`205s`) -> `0.00%` CER loss vs `1.35 GB` `FP32`!** |
| `V3_Q2_0` 2-Bit `DiT` Raw PTQ | `138.90 MB` (`9.71x`) | `3.30` | `100.00%` *(Static)* | `87.94%` | `16.657` | **Complete ODE collapse** before `PRIMAL` |
| **`V3_Q2_0 + Velocity-Field PRIMAL`** | **`138.90 MB` (`9.71x`)** | **`3.30`** | **`6.78%` (`-93.2%`!)** | **`4.68%`** | **`8.497`** | **`164,654` flips (`4.2 min` CFM distill): `100% -> 6.78%` WER!** |

---

## How WeSolved 2-Bit Diffusion (`DiT`) Quantization Collapse

1. **Protecting `adaLN-Zero` Modulation Gates:** Every `DiT` block uses an `adaLN-Zero` linear projection to regress `6` per-channel shift, scale, and residual-gate vectors from the continuous ODE time embedding `t in [0, 1]`. Crushing `adaLN` to 2 bits corrupts feature variance across all `22` blocks and `16` Euler ODE steps. Keeping `adaLN` + I/O projections in 4-bit `V3_P4_0` (`4.50 bpw`) while compressing all **`188.7M` `DiT` Attention (`Q/K/V/O`), Feed-Forward, and `ConvNeXt V2` CNN weights** to **2-bit `V3_Q2_0` (`2.25 bpw`)** packs the `1.35 GB` model into **`138.90 MB`** (`9.71x` compression).
2. **Trajectory Velocity-Field Shadowless `PRIMAL`:** Instead of unrolling backpropagation through all `16` ODE steps (which explodes VRAM and vanishes gradients), we cache `108` exact `FP32` teacher `(x_t, t, v_cond, v_uncond)` snapshots across Sway-Sampled timesteps `t in [0, 1]` and train both the 2-bit `V3_Q2_0` `DiT` body and 4-bit `V3_P4_0` `adaLN` codes/scales directly in integer space (`0` `FP32` shadow weights, `0.95` leaky `int8` vote decay, Adafactor Gauss-Newton preconditioning) to match the Classifier-Free Guided velocity vector field (`ema_loss: 2.128 -> 0.456` in `251.8s`).

# antzoki-mini-tts GGUF (Q4_K_M)

CPU build of [itzune/antzoki-mini-tts](https://huggingface.co/itzune/antzoki-mini-tts), a Basque
(*euskara*) fine-tune of [Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air)
(0.6B, DualAR, 44.1 kHz codec, zero-shot voice cloning), as a bundle for the Audio8 llama.cpp
runtime. It runs with no Python and no GPU.

> **The bundle needs the Audio8-patched llama.cpp**, not stock llama.cpp, Ollama or LM Studio.
> The runtime does the text processing, DualAR generation, voice cloning and codec decoding.

## Files

| File | Type | Size |
|---|---|---:|
| `models/slow-q4_k_m.gguf` | slow AR (24 layers), Q4_K_M | 387 MiB |
| `models/fast-q4_k_m.gguf` | fast AR (4 layers, 10 codebooks), Q4_K_M | 46 MiB |
| `models/codebook_embeddings.f32` | codebook embeddings, F32 | 140 MiB |
| `models/audio8-realistic-codec-f32.gguf` | audio codec, F32 | 1.26 GiB |
| `audio8-runtime.json` | bundle manifest read by the runtime | |

Only the two AR models are quantized. The RoPE tables and the codec stay F32 because the runtime
requires it, so the codec is most of the download. The model width (896) is not a multiple of
256, so Q4_K_M uses Q5_0/Q8_0 for about half of its tensors.

## Usage

```bash
# 1. Build the runtime (once). CPU build with this machine's SIMD + OpenMP.
git clone https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp.git
git -C llama.cpp checkout d854d98bae598388ecea1ed84396587e5edc326d
python3 Audio8_TTS/llama_cpp/prepare.py --source llama.cpp
cmake -S llama.cpp -B build-cpu -G "Unix Makefiles" -C Audio8_TTS/llama_cpp/cmake/common.cmake \
  -DGGML_NATIVE=ON -DGGML_OPENMP=ON -DAUDIO8_CODEC_OPENMP=ON '-DCMAKE_INSTALL_RPATH=$ORIGIN/../lib'
cmake --build build-cpu --parallel --target llama-tts

# 2. Download the bundle and the Basque text normalizer
hf download itzune/antzoki-mini-tts-GGUF --local-dir antzoki-gguf
hf download itzune/antzoki-mini-tts eu_normalize.py --local-dir .

# 3. Synthesize. Normalize the text first: numbers, dates and abbreviations become words.
TEXT=$(python3 -c 'from eu_normalize import normalize; print(normalize("Bihar goizean, zortzietan, Bilboko geltokian elkartuko gara."))')
build-cpu/bin/llama-tts --audio8-model-dir antzoki-gguf --text "$TEXT" --output out.wav \
  --gpu-layers 0 --threads 16 --max-frames 512

# Voice cloning: 10–15 s of clean speech plus its exact transcript
build-cpu/bin/llama-tts --audio8-model-dir antzoki-gguf --text "$TEXT" --output clone.wav \
  --gpu-layers 0 --threads 16 --max-frames 512 \
  --reference-audio ref.wav --reference-text "Erreferentzian esaten den testu zehatza."
```

`llama-tts` does not overwrite an existing `--output` file. When generation reaches
`--max-frames` without an end of speech (a runaway), it exits with an error. Run it again with
another `--seed`.

## Quality and speed

Measured on CPU with 8 sentences that are not in the training data, with a held-out reference voice
and without a reference, and 3 seeds each.

| Bundle | Size | Speaker SIM ↑ | Runaways, with ref | Runaways, no ref | RTF (with ref / no ref) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| F32 | 3.6 GB | 0.932 | 1/24 | 3/24 | 7.9 / 7.1 |
| **Q4_K_M (this repo)** | 1.9 GB | **0.940** | **0/24** | 4/24 | 3.7 / 2.7 |
| Q4_0 | 1.8 GB | 0.923 | 3/24 | 7/24 | 3.4 / 2.4 |

The Q4_K_M and F32 results are within noise of each other, and Q4_K_M is 2–2.6× faster. RTF is
seconds of compute per second of audio, measured with 4 jobs sharing the CPU. One job with 16
threads runs at about 2 RTF: a 5 s sentence with a reference takes 2.8 s of AR, 4.7 s of codec
and 3.3 s of reference encoding. CPU synthesis is therefore slower than real time, and the F32
codec is the bottleneck.

## Limitations

The limitations of the [original model](https://huggingface.co/itzune/antzoki-mini-tts) apply.
It was trained on about 9 hours of read speech, and it mispronounces some rare words and names
(for example *Antton*). There is no speed parameter: the pace follows the reference. Without a
reference, the voice and the pace change with every seed.

## Reproduce

The conversion and quantization scripts are in
[github.com/itzune/antzoki-mini-tts](https://github.com/itzune/antzoki-mini-tts) (`scripts/gguf/`):
`convert_eu.py` (F32 bundle), `quantize_eu.sh` (Q4_K_M) and `eval_gguf.py` (the table above).

## License

Apache-2.0, like the base model. See `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`.

# antzoki-mini-tts

Basque (*euskara*) text-to-speech: a supervised fine-tune of the slow AR branch (fast AR kept frozen) of
[Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air](https://huggingface.co/Edge0/Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air)
(0.6B, DualAR, 44.1 kHz codec, zero-shot voice cloning). Basque is not one of the base
model's 23 languages, so this release adapts it to a new language.

> **Status: experimental.** Trained on about 9 hours of read speech from one corpus. Listen to
> the samples before you use it, and expect errors on rare words, acronyms and code-switching.

## Usage

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Edge0-AI/Audio8_TTS && cd Audio8_TTS
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

```python
import sys, soundfile as sf, torch
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoProcessor

repo = "itzune/antzoki-mini-tts"
sys.path.insert(0, hf_hub_download(repo, "eu_normalize.py").rsplit("/", 1)[0])
from eu_normalize import normalize          # same normalizer as in training

processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(repo, trust_remote_code=True)
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(repo, trust_remote_code=True, dtype=torch.bfloat16).cuda().eval()

text = normalize("Donostiako zinemaldia 1953an sortu zen.")   # -> "... mila bederatziehun eta berrogeita hamahiruan ..."
inputs = processor(text=[text], return_tensors="pt")
# voice cloning: processor(text=[text], reference_audio=["ref.wav"], reference_text=["exact transcript"], return_tensors="pt")
inputs = {k: v.cuda() for k, v in inputs.items()}
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=True, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95,
                     top_k=50, return_dict_in_generate=True)
wav, lengths = model.decode_audio(out.codes)
sf.write("out.wav", wav[0, : int(lengths[0])].float().cpu().numpy(), model.config.codec_sample_rate)
```

Or with the CLI from the Audio8 repo:
`python audio8_tts_infer.py --model itzune/antzoki-mini-tts --text "..." [--reference-audio ref.wav --reference-text "..."] --output out.wav`

CPU without Python or GPU: the llama.cpp GGUF build (Q4_K_M) is in [itzune/antzoki-mini-tts-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/itzune/antzoki-mini-tts-GGUF).

**Always normalize the text with `eu_normalize.normalize()`.** The model never saw digits
during training: numbers become Basque words that keep their case suffix
(`2008an` → `bi mila eta zortzian`, `1950eko` → `mila bederatziehun eta berrogeita hamarreko`).
Keep each input under about 150 characters.

## Training

| | |
|---|---|
| Data | [OpenSLR 76](https://www.openslr.org/76/): crowdsourced Basque read speech. After filtering: 6811 training utterances (9.1 h), 50 speakers |
| Held out | speakers `euf_07505`, `eum_01523`, used for evaluation and never trained on |
| Audio prep | silence trimming, resampled to 44.1 kHz, loudness set to −20 LUFS (−1 dBFS peak), speaking-rate outlier filter |
| Voice cloning | 61% of training rows paired with another utterance of the same speaker as the reference prompt |
| Method | slow AR branch trained, fast AR (acoustic detail) frozen, bf16, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, 1× RTX 5090 (24 GB) |
| Hyper-params | learning_rate=1e-5, num_train_epochs=2, batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=4, warmup_ratio=0.03, lr_scheduler_type=cosine, weight_decay=0.01, extra: `--load_best_model_at_end true --metric_for_best_model eval_loss --greater_is_better false` |
| Pipeline | https://github.com/itzune/antzoki-mini-tts (Audio8_TTS @ `aef426d`) |

## Evaluation

Teacher-forced loss on 200 utterances from the held-out speakers (lower is better).

| Model | eval loss | slow loss | fast loss | slow acc |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| base (Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air) | 12.730 | 5.423 | 7.308 | 0.102 |
| audio8_eu_sft_v2 | 9.088 | 3.803 | 5.285 | 0.176 |
| **audio8_eu_sft_v4 (this release)** | 9.183 | 3.806 | 5.378 | 0.177 |

A first run (2e-5 learning rate, 6 epochs) reached its best held-out loss after about 250 steps
and then overfit: OpenSLR 76 has many speakers reading the same sentences. This release uses the same short, early-stopped schedule with the fast AR frozen: its loss is slightly higher than the fully fine-tuned run, but it sounds and measures about the same and had fewer runaway generations when cloning.

**Voice cloning and robustness** (8 new sentences × 2 held-out reference voices + no reference, 8 seeds). SIM = cosine similarity of WavLM speaker embeddings between the output and the reference (real recordings: 0.97 same speaker, 0.673 different speakers). A runaway has no end of speech or a speaking rate below 8 characters/s.

| Model | SIM ↑ | runaway, with ref | runaway, no ref |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| base (Audio8-TTS-Realistic-Air) | 0.968 | 8/128 (6%) | 5/64 (8%) |
| this model | 0.957 | 4/128 (3%) | 8/64 (12%) |

## Samples

No reference audio (the model picks a voice):

- **Bihar goizean, zortzietan, Bilboko geltokian elkartuko gara.**
  <audio controls src="samples/noref_s01.wav"></audio>
- **Euskara Europako hizkuntzarik zaharrenetakoa da, eta oraindik bizirik dirau.**
  <audio controls src="samples/noref_s02.wav"></audio>

## Limitations and responsible use

- Small single-domain corpus (read sentences): spontaneous or expressive speech, long inputs,
  dialects and code-switching are out of distribution.
- Acronyms and alphanumeric names (`U2`, `AP-68`) are read with Basque digit names.
- Some generations run away (no end of speech, long silences or babbling), as with the base
  model. Check the duration and regenerate with another seed when it makes no sense for the
  text; `scripts/say.py` in the GitHub repo does this automatically.
- There is no speed parameter. With a reference, the model copies most of the reference's pace;
  without one, the pace varies from seed to seed.
- The palatal *tt* / *dd* sounds (*Antton*, *pottoka*) are almost absent from the training data
  and usually come out wrong. Having the word in the reference helps only sometimes.
- Voice cloning can imitate real people. Do not clone a voice without the speaker's consent,
  and do not use this model to impersonate anyone or to deceive.

# MusicGen Small

Meta's MusicGen Small text-to-music model, exported for loom.cpp. Family 14: a text description in, EnCodec tokens out -- pair it with `encodec-32khz-loom` for audio.

This is a [loom.cpp](https://github.com/loom-ai-org/loom.cpp) export: a single self-describing GGUF
that carries its own graph topologies, tokenizer (if any) and driver script, produced by
[loom-exporter](https://github.com/loom-ai-org/loom-exporter).

## Original model

Exported from [`facebook/musicgen-small`](https://huggingface.co/facebook/musicgen-small). Weights are unmodified; this repo packages the same parameters into
loom.cpp's GGUF format.

## License

`cc-by-nc-4.0`, inherited from the base model above.

## Language(s)

`en`

## Usage

Run it with [loom-py](https://github.com/loom-ai-org/loom-py) -- `loom-py-rt` on PyPI:

```sh
pip install -U "loom-py-rt[hub]>=1.0.0"
```

```python
import loom

model = loom.Model.from_pretrained("loom-ai-org/musicgen-small-loom")

# The prompt DESCRIBES the music -- genre, instruments, mood. What comes back is EnCodec TOKENS, not
# audio: frame-major, 4 codebooks wide, 50 frames per second, so max_new_tokens=250 is five seconds.
codes = model.text2codes.infer("80s pop track with bassy drums and synth", max_new_tokens=250, seed=1)
print(len(codes), "frames x", len(codes[0]), "codebooks")

# The second half of the pair, in a repo of its own: the codec this model was trained with.
codec = loom.Model.from_pretrained("loom-ai-org/encodec-32khz-loom")
audio = codec.codes2speech.infer(codes)
print(len(audio), "samples at", audio.sample_rate, "Hz =", round(audio.duration, 2), "s")
audio.save("out.wav")

# Nothing goes between those two calls. Both files declare the width of a frame:
print(model.hparam("codec.n_codebooks"), "==", codec.hparam("codec.n_codebooks"))

# This model SAMPLES by default, with classifier-free guidance; `seed=` pins a take, and
# temperature=0 decodes greedily (transformers' generate(do_sample=False), code for code).
print(model.hparam("sampling.top_k"), model.hparam("sampling.guidance_scale", "f32"))
```

### Streaming

```python
# Live: the codes as they are drawn, each piece decoded as it arrives -- the two streams chained
# (loom.cpp ADR-102). Play each piece as it comes.
sizes = [len(piece) for piece in codec.codes2speech.stream(model.text2codes.stream("80s pop track with bassy drums and synth", max_new_tokens=100, seed=1))]
print(len(sizes), "pieces,", sum(sizes), "samples")
```

### The layer underneath

The call above is the high-level door: one per task, named for the modality pair it maps between, with
the windowing, sampling and assembly this model needs already applied. Under it, `model.infer(...)`
passes your arguments straight to the driver this GGUF embeds -- which is where you go for a knob the
door does not name.

`model.driver_source` prints that driver, including a header comment documenting every argument it
accepts for this model, and is the authority on it. See [loom-py](https://github.com/loom-ai-org/loom-py) for the API and
[loom.cpp](https://github.com/loom-ai-org/loom.cpp) for what the engine does between the two.

## Known limitations

**This model does not produce audio.** It emits four streams of EnCodec tokens, and [`encodec-32khz-loom`](https://huggingface.co/loom-ai-org/encodec-32khz-loom) -- the codec it was trained with -- turns them into 32 kHz mono audio. The usage snippet above is the whole of the joining.

**The prompt describes the music; it is not lyrics.** Genre, instruments, tempo and mood in English, through the T5 vocabulary this file carries. MusicGen Small makes no vocals.

**It samples, at the settings `transformers` uses for this checkpoint**: `top_k 50` and classifier-free guidance at `3.0`. (Meta's own `audiocraft` library samples with `top_k 250`; this file follows the checkpoint's Hugging Face generation config.) Two runs give two takes; `seed=` pins one, and `temperature=0` decodes greedily, which reproduces `transformers`' `generate(do_sample=False)` code for code.

`max_new_tokens` counts **audio frames** at 50 per second, so 250 is five seconds. The default is 1496 frames, about 30 s, which is the checkpoint's own generation length and its training clip length. The decoder's 2048 positions cap one call at 2045 frames (40.9 s).

Guidance costs a second decoder pass at every step, so it roughly doubles the work. `guidance_scale=1.0` turns it off: faster, and the music follows the prompt less closely. On a 4-thread laptop-class CPU, two seconds of music took about 27 s with guidance and 14 s without; a GPU or more cores helps.

**Expect lo-fi sound; that comes from the model, not from this export.** MusicGen generates music as a 2.2 kbps EnCodec stream: four 2048-entry codebooks at 50 frames a second. That is enough for style, rhythm and instrumentation, and it sounds about like an old radio. This file's codes match `transformers` exactly, and the codec matches it to 3e-5, so a sharper result would have to come from a larger MusicGen checkpoint, not a different runtime.

Mono and text-conditioned only. The melody-conditioned and stereo MusicGen checkpoints are different models and are not covered by this file. 2.1 GB, F32.

# AuralGuard: Multi-View One-Class Learning for Generalizable and Calibrated Detection of AI-Generated Speech in the Wild

Official checkpoint repository, standardized evaluation manifests, and reproducible artifact logs for the paper:  
**"AuralGuard: Multi-View One-Class Learning for Generalizable and Calibrated Detection of AI-Generated Speech in the Wild"**  
*Target: Elsevier Machine Learning with Applications (MLWA) / IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security (T-IFS)*

- 📄 **Manuscript Status:** Preprint currently under peer review. The manuscript PDF is not hosted in this repository; contact the authors for an academic copy.
- 💻 **Official Code Repository:** [github.com/MIHMahmudEli/auralguard](https://github.com/MIHMahmudEli/auralguard.git)
- 👥 **Authors:** Mohsin Ibna Hossain, Md. Muttakin, Sadman Hasan Miraj, and Md. Khairul Alam Mazumder* (*Corresponding Author*, khairul@aiub.edu)
- 🏛️ **Affiliation:** Department of Computer Science, American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB)
- 📋 **Evaluation Manifests:** Hosted under [`manifests/`](manifests/)
- 📜 **Reproducible Artifact Logs:** Hosted under [`logs/`](logs/)

---

## 📊 Empirical Benchmark Results

Trained strictly once on **ASVspoof 2019 LA** and evaluated zero-shot out-of-domain across all benchmarks. Metrics report point estimates with 95% non-parametric bootstrap confidence intervals ($B=1,000$).
